Es la identidad del producto de senos, l: It is the product-of-sines identity, the inverse of the previous topic's. It says that multiplying two sines does not give a sine: it gives two, at the sum and the difference of the frequencies. So the modulated signal has three lines: the carrier $f_c$ (with amplitude 1) and two sidebands at $f_c \pm f_m$, each with amplitude $m/2$. The modulator is not heard at its frequency: it appears at the sides of the carrier.

Hasta ahora los parámetros de un seno —a: So far a sine's parameters, amplitude and frequency, were fixed numbers, or an envelope changing slowly. Modulating is moving one of them with another sine. If the amplitude is moved, there is tremolo; if the frequency is moved, vibrato. And if the moving sine goes as fast as the sounding one, new frequencies appear: the identity of [[son-batidos|the topic on beats]] predicts them, and the [[son-armonicos|harmonics]] explain them. Out of that came the synthesiser that sounded through a whole decade.
John Chowning, un compositor que trabaja: John Chowning, a composer working at Stanford's artificial intelligence laboratory, discovered in 1967 that an exaggeratedly fast vibrato stopped sounding like vibrato and became a new timbre. He published FM synthesis in 1973; Stanford patented it and no American company wanted it. Yamaha licensed it, and in 1983 brought out the DX7: the first highly successful digital synthesiser, two hundred thousand sold, with the electric piano, the bass and the bells that are on almost every record of the 1980s. For years the patent was the university's most profitable, ahead of the biotechnology ones.

Si $f_m = f_c$, las bandas caen en $0$,: If $f_m = f_c$, the sidebands fall at $0$, $f_c$, $2f_c$, $3f_c$…: multiples of the carrier, that is, harmonics. If $f_m$ is $2f_c$, only the odd ones come out; if it is an odd multiple like $1{.}41 f_c$, frequencies come out that are not multiples: it sounds like a bell or a gong. It is FM synthesis, and with it were built the electric pianos, the basses and the bells of almost all the music of the 1980s.
